summary: The config flies: the base ship survives its own launch, both routes reach the band, and the module can only come home aerobraked — but the capacity window that carries the endgame is 2.7% wide, the module needs two skims from the top rather than one, the full hold is 1.23x the ship's mass instead of the promised 2x, and no measured configuration anywhere in the grid survives an unstaged braking pass.

findings.claim: GDD 2.2 states a 32% window between the full hold's plunge peak (203.7) and the module's (268.8), bounded by a rule rather than by how finely anyone searched, and calls that why it is safe to build on.
findings.measured: Flown at the commit floor the window is (217.8, 223.7) — 2.7% wide. The module's best skimmed peak from the top is 217.8 and its bottom-sample plunge is 223.7, and the whole shield ladder (219 / 221 / 223) is squeezed inside those two numbers. The full hold's plunge is not the lower bound at all: it peaks at 104.3 / 128.6 / 163.4, less than half the module's, so ordinary cargo is nowhere near the constraint. The balancer's own note records the window closing to 0.8% at dry mass 900 and going negative at 1,000, so the mechanic survives on a 100 kg margin in a parameter nobody is guarding.

findings.claim: GDD 2.2's table and 2.6's finale describe the module coming home on one braking pass — 196.5 against a ~235 capacity — and 2.6 calls the finale an aerobraking flight of that shape.
findings.measured: From the top sample the module peaks at 335.5 on a plunge, 243.2 with one skim and 217.8 with two. 243.2 is above every purchasable capacity (219 / 221 / 223), so one skim does not bring it home from where it actually hangs; two does. From the middle the same pattern holds — 268.5 / 224.4 / 213.9, with the one-skim figure again above the ladder. Only from the bottom sample does a single skim work (208.2). The finale is a three-cycle descent, not a two-cycle one.

findings.claim: GDD 2.2 makes staged-versus-unstaged braking a real choice: the hull takes each pass at 3x heat but keeps the engine for between-pass periapsis control.
findings.measured: The exploration grid satisfies unstaged_pass_survivable in 8.0% of 5,184 configurations — the lowest rate of any target, and not one of the twelve best-scoring worlds satisfies it (every top entry reports false, with unstaged peaks of 247, 311 and 376 against capacities in the low hundreds). The verification sweep does report the crew's own shallow unstaged pass surviving at 71 and 78 for bottom and middle, and no row at all for the top — so the choice exists in shallow passes low in the band and vanishes exactly where the endgame is flown. This is the rule, not the numbers: 92% of the space cannot buy it.

findings.claim: GDD 2.5 and 2.6 both lean on a full hold roughly doubling the rocket's mass; 2.6 sizes the module against that as 'a maxed hold's mass budget'.
findings.measured: Six slots at the catalog's 30.43 kg/slot is a 182.6 kg hold on an 800 kg ship — 1.23x. The consequences are all measured, not argued: the full hold lands at 3.22 m/s where an empty ship lands at 2.91, a 0.31 m/s spread across the entire greed decision; storage tier 2 moves ten slots' touchdown to 3.42 m/s, still soft on the base canopy with no purchase required; and the full hold's plunge peaks at 163.4 from the top against the empty ship's 147.8. Satisfying the doubling from dry mass needs 183 kg, a staged ballistic coefficient of 37 — under the ~50 floor where first air contact erases the orbit and the skim mechanic ceases to exist. The catalog is the only lever that closes it.

findings.claim: GDD 2.2 and Revision 3 withdraw the old 2-4 pass cost optimum and assert one pass is the cheapest descent under every ablation keying measured, making multi-pass a feasibility rule rather than a cost rule.
findings.measured: Confirmed in all twelve descent rows: cheapest_pass_count is 1 everywhere, from 7.3% of plate (top, empty) to 40.9% (bottom, endgame haul), and cost rises monotonically with pass count in every row — the bottom full hold runs 8.8 / 15.2 / 22.1 / 29.9 / 38.6 / 72.2 / 253.7 across 1 through 16 passes. The grid agrees that the benefit saturates: skim_benefit_saturates holds in 88.9% of configurations, the highest rate of any target, and every measured multiplier array is flat after index 1 or 2. The design's own withdrawal of the cost target is the correct call and should not be reopened.

findings.claim: GDD 2.5 makes the first tank upgrade the buy that turns a hop into a stay, with the base ship able to circularise only at the floor and arriving with nothing to deorbit on.
findings.measured: The base ship circularises at the bottom sample with 6.9% of tank (109.83 kg) and at the middle with 2.9% (46.36 kg), and cannot circularise at the top at all ('out of fuel before circularising', 19.2% left on the arc). The middle sample's 2.9% is a circularisation the sweep scores as reached but which leaves no deorbit budget — a route the player can take that strands them, one band above where the design says it should already be impossible. The arc margins are healthy throughout: 29.4% / 23.8% / 18.0%, with EVA windows of 125.9 / 202.1 / 368.3 s, so the arc is genuinely the first launch's route as designed and GDD 4.5's 97-second question is answered generously at 125.9 s.

findings.claim: GDD 2.3 requires parachute_area_m2 to be a stated constant so the predicted descent speed is a claim the flight can contradict, and predicts 4.4 m/s at base storage with a full hold.
findings.measured: With area 630 m2 at Cd 1.8 stated in the params, the closed form predicts 3.23 m/s and the integrator lands the full hold at 3.22 m/s at all three sample altitudes — delta 0.01 m/s, spread across bands 0.00, independent true. The tautology is genuinely gone. But the predicted number is 3.22, not the GDD's 4.4, because the mass under the canopy is 982.6 kg rather than the ~2x hold the document assumes — the same shortfall as the doubling finding, seen through the chute. The module lands at 6.83 m/s on the base canopy and needs parachute tier 2 (1,250 m2, 4.84 m/s) for a soft touchdown, so the Parachute track is what buys a pristine delivery.

findings.claim: The design assumes a workable fuel margin is a tuning matter once the world is locked.
findings.measured: fuel_margin_sane holds in 18.7% of 5,184 grid configurations and launch_survives_itself in 34.0% — the second and third rarest targets after unstaged_pass_survivable at 8.0%. The crew's config hits both, and the climb peaks at 50.0 / 47.5 / 46.7 bar units against capacity 219, reproducing GDD 2.2's stated 47.5 exactly at the middle sample. That is a real achievement on a thin part of the space, and it is also a warning: the locked planet sits somewhere only a fifth of worlds reach, so any future change to radius, gravity or sea-level density is very likely to break the ascent rather than adjust it.

proposed_changes.reason: Raising the shipping slice's mean piece mass to about 133 kg makes a six-slot hold 800 kg on an 800 kg ship — GDD 2.5's doubling satisfied from the catalog rather than from a dry mass that would delete aerobraking — and loads the canopy to 4.11 m/s, mid-soft-band, at the cost of a 4.4x revaluation pass across every piece below 203,333 m.

Dropping the base capacity below the module's two-skim peak from the top (217.8) while staying far above the full hold's worst plunge (163.4) widens the useful ladder span and makes the shield track buy something measurable, at the cost of requiring tier 1 before any module attempt at all.

With the base at 210 the ladder becomes 210 / 215 / 220, every tier still under the module's 223.7 bottom-sample plunge and the top two above its 217.8 two-skim peak, so the purchase decides the finale instead of three near-identical numbers sharing a 2.7% band.

Places tier 1 below the module's two-skim requirement so the first shield buy is a real step rather than a 2-unit rounding, and keeps the whole track under the plunge ceiling the GDD makes non-negotiable.

The Parachute track is the only thing standing between a 6.83 m/s module touchdown and a pristine delivery, so it is carrying the endgame's landing gate and is underpriced relative to the heat shield at 700; costs an earlier canopy upgrade in the mid campaign.

Trimming base tank capacity pushes the middle sample's 2.9% circularisation below the reachable line so the base ship can only circularise at the floor as GDD 2.5 describes, removing a route that strands the player, at the cost of shaving the bottom sample's orbit margin from 6.9% toward ~4%.

confidence_notes: The simulator is a point mass with a perfect pilot. Every skim altitude in the committed_descents table was found by scanning — the module's two-skim survival from the top rests on hitting 24,585 m, and a human flying by the CHUTE lamp and an aim indicator has no instrument that reads that number. The 2.7% capacity window is measured, but its playable width is smaller than its measured width by an amount only a human can determine.

The unstaged_braking table has rows for bottom and middle only — no top-sample row was flown. I read the missing row as unflown rather than as a failure, so the claim that the unstaged choice vanishes at the top of the band is inference from the grid's 8.0% satisfaction rate, not a direct measurement of this config.

The 133 kg/slot proposal is arithmetic on the catalog's own mean, not a flown result. It closes the doubling and the canopy margin simultaneously in closed form; whether the resulting value economy still clears the shop in 12-15 runs has not been simulated, and the balancer's pricing notes would all need recomputing against it.

The heat capacity ladder proposal (210 / 215 / 220) is derived from the same committed_descents peaks the current ladder was fitted to, so it inherits whatever bias those measurements carry. If the module's 217.8 two-skim peak moves under a different scan resolution, the proposed ladder breaks in the same direction the current one does — it is a wider spacing of the same fragile window, not an escape from it.

I did not evaluate whether one skim versus two changes how the finale feels. The measured difference is roughly six minutes of wall clock per pass at warp and one more heat cycle at an escalating toll; whether a three-cycle finale reads as a climactic sequence or as a chore is exactly the judgement the charter says belongs to a human.
